findings.title: kill() is never called on unhealthy spawn processes (isinstance check is always False)
findings.body: `_ensure_processes_alive` only kills the old worker if `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes here are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which produces `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` objects. `SpawnProcess` derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.context.Process` (which is what the module-level `multiprocessing.Process` alias resolves to), so the isinstance check is always False and `kill()` is never invoked. The previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`) the old process keeps running while a replacement is started for the same shards, so two processes concurrently flush the same Redis shards and produce duplicate/fragmented segments to `buffered-segments`, and leaked processes accumulate on every restart. Use `process.kill()` guarded by `hasattr`/`BaseProcess` instead.

findings.title: join() aborts the shutdown loop, leaving the remaining processes unterminated
findings.body: In `join()`, when the deadline has passed the loop `break`s out before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for the remaining entries of `self.processes`. With more than one flusher process, a timed-out join therefore terminates only the processes iterated before the deadline expired; the rest are left running and continue flushing segments while the consumer is shutting down/rebalancing. (Additionally, `remaining_time` is computed but never used, and the `terminate()` call itself is dead for spawn processes because of the same `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` problem.) Terminate every process unconditionally after the wait loop.

findings.title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
findings.body: `test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at line 15, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") does nothing. The test still relies on the flusher thread having produced the message before `step.join()` returns, so the intended synchronization is absent and the test remains timing-dependent/flaky. Use a real sleep (e.g. `from time import sleep as real_sleep` captured before patching, as `test_flusher.py` does) or poll until `messages` is non-empty.

findings.title: New multi-process flusher test only asserts bookkeeping, never exercises flushing across shards
findings.body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` creates 4 partitions with `flusher_processes=2` but never submits a message and never asserts that segments from all 4 shards are produced. It only checks `len(flusher.processes)`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and the total shard count. The behaviour this PR actually changes — several shards being flushed by one worker, and all shards being covered by the shard->process mapping — is untested. Consider submitting spans for each partition and asserting that one produced message per shard arrives, and that `process_to_shards_map` is a partition of `assigned_shards` (no duplicates/omissions).

findings.title: Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` left behind
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). Dead code that duplicates restart logic is a maintenance hazard — a future caller would restart a whole process group from a single shard id. Remove it.

findings.title: Class docstring claims one process per shard and documents a non-existent param
findings.body: The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))`, and the consumer CLI defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, so the normal configuration is a single process handling all shards. The docstring also still documents `:param topic:` which is not an argument, and does not document the new `max_processes` argument. This misleads operators about the default parallelism.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag key and high-cardinality tag value for shard tags
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `shard=<comma-joined shard list>` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses the key `shards` for the same value. Dashboards/alerts filtering on `shard` will silently miss `wait_produce`, and a comma-joined value such as `"0,4,8"` is a different tag value for every shard-to-process assignment, which breaks aggregation by shard and inflates metric cardinality whenever partition assignment changes. Pick one key and emit a stable, low-cardinality value (e.g. the process index) or emit per-shard series.

findings.title: A new SpansBuffer (and its Redis clients) is created in the parent on every restart without releasing the old one
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shards` constructs a fresh `SpansBuffer(shards)` and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The parent process keeps using these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so each unhealthy-process restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process) leaves the previous buffer's Redis connections unclosed in the parent. Reuse the existing buffer for the process index, or close the old one before replacing it.
